Sports.title: Ruthless England dethrone shambolic India as world's best T20 side - after brutal Jos Buttler leads hosts to thumping win
Sports.content:
Ruthless England dethrone shambolic India as world's best T20 side - after brutal Jos Buttler leads hosts to thumping win

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Jos Buttler struck just his second Twenty20 hundred of a 15-year England career as India were spectacularly dethroned as the world's No 1-ranked side.

Buttler, 35, had gone 18 innings without even a 50, but put a rabble of an Indian team to the sword during a national record 233-run partnership with his successor as captain Harry Brook.

England now sit atop the ICC's table after Buttler's career-best 131 from 64 balls, coupled with Brook's unbeaten 95 off 45 condemned India to a 56-run defeat and ended their incredible unbroken reign of 1602 days as No 1.

This was England's 20th win in 23 matches since Brook took over at the start of last summer, but India - whose late arrival, after being stuck in Southampton traffic delayed the start by an hour - have been as bad as they have been good.

In a worrying precursor to next year's Ashes Test, it took Shreyas Iyer's team one and a half hours to complete the six-mile journey to the Utilita Bowl from the Leonardo Royal hotel in Southampton.

'We thought that we would be reaching in 20 minutes, but it was out of our control,' Iyer said.

Jos Buttler was the catalyst for England's T20 win over India on Saturday at the Utilita Bowl

Buttler scored a career best 131 as England inflicted a 53-run defeat on India in Southampton

The tardiness was symptomatic of India's display. Having got Brook to the crease early on a belting Utilita Bowl pitch, they gifted England's in-form batsman a life on three when Shivam Dube looked to have plenty of time to clutch a skier just outside the fielding circle, but never got there.

India would also shell Brook on 90 and Buttler immediately after he got to three figures - an innings he admitted was inspired by fear of the axe.

'When you go a long time without scoring runs you think the guys at the top might be thinking: It's time to move him on,' Buttler said.

'In a weird way that gave me a lot more freedom today – if I was going to fail, I'll do it on my own terms. Days like this feel amazing. I think what I've missed is that feeling, the feeling of contributing to a series win, to winning games for England.

'I've just missed batting, the feeling of being in control and playing well. There's been days where you wonder if you'll ever score 100 again in an England shirt, and I'm delighted to be able to do that.'

Each of the second-wicket pair hit eight sixes as India's lack of an attack spearhead - the rested Jasprit Bumrah has arrived for the one-day internationals that begin on Tuesday - and a dearth of quality spin in the tourists' ranks told.

It forced Iyer to bowl out Arshdeep Singh early in the hunt for an elusive breakthrough, and throw the ball to part-timer Dube at the death as England's 213 runs from the final 15 overs took them to 257 for three, their third largest T20 total.

Seasoned observers suggest that the Indian hierarchy have identified the areas which need urgent attention. Yet anyone who has been following the series could have told them it is their batting, bowling and fielding.

Careering from one disaster to another, the shambolic fielding display concluded with the farcical failure to run Brook out from the final ball.

'It definitely hurts, but I feel like it's a great learning for me as a captain and for other players playing here for the first time. England played exceptional cricket throughout in all three departments,' Iyer said.

Hours after their board secretary Devajit Saikia confirmed the impending launch of an England style review into their under-par displays, India axed their precocious batting talent Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, answering post-match calls from the stands in Nottingham and Bristol to bring back World Cup star Sanju Samson.

Samson, player of the World Cup four months ago, returned fire on his comeback, but could not get beyond the power play, becoming one of Sam Curran's three wickets.

And even though left-handers Ishan Kishan and Tilak Varma hit rapid half-centuries, the damage had already been done.

India reached 109 for two at the halfway stage, yet still needed a touch under 15 runs an over to avoid another humiliation to go with their record 125-run defeat at Trent Bridge.

Iyer was out immediately after the drinks break, and when Kishan followed to a brilliant, diving catch in the deep two overs later, India's chance of victory according to WinViz was a smidgen over one per cent.

India breached 200 for the first time in the series, but for the first time since February 2022, when Harry Kane's England goal tally stood at a mere 48 and Jude Bellingham was yet to get off the mark - they were no longer the best 20-over team on the planet.

Sports.title: Mo Salah is wanted by MLS side Sporting Kansas City, Everton keen on Jacob Murphy and Man City complete £10m Jeremy Monga deal: WINDOW WATCH
Sports.content:
Mo Salah is wanted by MLS side Sporting Kansas City, Everton keen on Jacob Murphy and Man City complete £10m Jeremy Monga deal: WINDOW WATCH

It's that time of the year again - the transfer window is now open until September 1 and it's sure to be a busy period with clubs looking to make big signings ahead of next season.

Here are today's latest developments from Simon Jones and the Daily Mail Sport team...

Wolves bolster attack

Wolves have completed the signing of Comoros international winger Rafiki Said from Standard Liege in a deal worth up to £7.7million.

He has signed a three year deal with the option of an extra year.

Leeds up for fight over Muharemovic

Leeds are rivalling Bournemouth and Sunderland for Sassuolo centre back Tarik Muharemovic.

The Bosnia international has been on Bournemouth's radar for the past year and they made enquiries in January.

Sassuolo rate the 23-year-old at around £30million, but previous club Juventus mantain a 50 per cent sell-on clause.

Leeds are keen to add a centre back after selling Pascal Struijk to Brighton.

Garnacho heading for the exit

Chelsea are ready to sell Alejandro Garnacho after a single season at the club.

Daily Mail Sport reported earlier this week that two Champions League clubs are among those showing interest in Garnacho, with former club Manchester United retaining a 10 per cent sell-on clause.

Garnacho, who is valued at £45million, has not been involved in those first sessions held by new boss Xabi Alonso, with club and player working to finalise his future.

Alejandro Garnacho is heading for the exit door at Stamford Bridge

Daily Mail Sport understand Chelsea would like to move the player on before their pre-season tour of Australia and Asia later this month.

Lampard lands Loum

Premier League new boys Coventry have completed the signing of Burnley winger Loum Tchaouna in a deal worth £20million.

The 22-year-old joined Burnley from Lazio for £13m last summer.

Daily Mail Sport understands that Frank Lampard's side are also finalising details on Aurele Amenda’s transfer from Eintracht Frankfurt.

The Swiss international will ratify his move once he has a medical after the World Cup.

Nypan heads back out on loan

Manchester City midfielder Sverre Nypan has joined Lommel on loan.

The 20-year-old Norway international endured a difficult loan at Middlesbrough last season.

Bournemouth defender set for Italy move

Bournemouth defender Alex Jimenez has travelled to Florence ahead of a medical with Fiorentina.

The Italians have a deal in place to take the full-back on loan with view to a £17.5million permanent transfer.

Jimenez was omitted from the Bournemouth first team in May pending an investigation into allegations posted against him on social media.

Bournemouth defender Alex Jimenez has travelled to Florence ahead of a medical with Fiorentina

He initially joined from AC Milan and Bournemouth activated their option to buy him at the start of this year.

However, they are now sending the 21-year-old back to Italy.

Hull interest in former player Zambrano

Hull City are looking to bring in Ecuador midfielder Oscar Zambrano from Maribor.

The 22-year-old had a previous spell with Hull on loan in 2024 but was hit with a ban for a positive drugs test while he had been playing for previous club Quito.

Zambrano is expected to arrive at the start of next week.

Hull City are looking to bring in Ecuador midfielder Oscar Zambrano from Maribor

Hull are also talking to Mjallby about left-back Elliot Stroud. The 24-year-old played for Sweden in the World Cup.

Cameroon internationals, Eintracht Frankfurt midfielder Eric Junior Dina Ebimbe and Lorient’s Arthur Avom are also under discussion but the Premier League new boys face competition on both.

Mo Salah wanted by MLS side

Mo Salah is wanted by Sporting Kansas City in the MLS.

The Egyptian is a free agent after leaving Liverpool and he and his representative Ramy Abbas are assessing options which are continuing to arrive from Saudi Arabia's Pro-League and Europe.

Mo Salah is wanted by Sporting Kansas City on a free after leaving Liverpool this summer

Kansas have made their pitch with a lucrative two year offer but recognise it may still be a long shot to tempt the 34-year-old across the Atlantic.

Everton keen on Newcastle star Murphy

Everton hold an interest in Newcastle United winger Jacob Murphy.

The 31-year-old has 12 months left on contract and could depart unless Newcastle are prepared to extend his contract.

He has been at Newcastle for nine years and has been an important part of Eddie Howe's squad.

Everton have signed Tyrique George from Chelsea and could yet re-sign Jack Grealish from Manchester City if a financial compromise can be found.

Everton hold an interest in Newcastle United's 31-year-old winger Jacob Murphy

They are determined to hold on to Iliman Ndiaye who has interest from a number of top clubs. He has three years left on his deal but so far he has failed to agree on new terms despite them being offered.

RB Leipzig have an interest in Tyler Dibling and Thierno Barry.

Man City sign teenage star Monga

Manchester City have completed the signing of Jeremy Monga from Leicester after pipping Arsenal to his signature.

The England U19 international has agreed a five-year deal, with City paying £10m for the winger who turned 17 on Friday.

Monga, who is the third-youngest player to ever play in the Premier League, said: 'When I became aware that Manchester City were interested, I knew instantly this was the right choice for me.

Manchester City have completed the signing of 17-year-old Jeremy Monga from Leicester

'For any young footballer, to become part of this amazing club is a dream come true. This has been the best club in England over the past 10 years.

'And it has also handed opportunities to players from the academy like Phil Foden and Nico O'Reilly, which shows that the pathway is there.'

Monga becomes new head coach Enzo Maresca's second signing of the summer after Elliott Anderson joined from Nottingham Forest for £116m.

Sports.title: Ken Bates dead at 94: Amazing life of controversial former Chelsea owner who saved the club, almost signed Graeme Souness, used to phone me up to rant about Todd Boehly and labelled Leeds fans 'morons'
Sports.content:
Ken Bates dead at 94: Amazing life of controversial former Chelsea owner who saved the club, almost signed Graeme Souness, used to phone me up to rant about Todd Boehly and labelled Leeds fans 'morons'

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

The emails have occasionally dropped from Ken Bates’ PAs in the past five or six years – either Tracey or Susan, relating that ‘Mr Bates’ had read something I had written. Would I call him so he might relate details that he considered ‘of journalistic interest’? The topic would be Chelsea. Always Chelsea. The club that was so clearly the love of his life.

Last year, he wanted to tell me he abhorred the way Todd Boehly and his acolytes - ‘money men’ rather than football men, as he saw them - had turned the club into a financial instrument. Though fans of Chelsea and Leeds United may scoff at the notion of Bates, who has died aged 94, pontificating on how clubs should be run, Stamford Bridge would be a very different place had it not been for him. Recency bias leads many to say that Roman Abramovich saved Chelsea. There is a very strong case to say that Bates did.

He fell out with so many people that he’d lost count, with bans from his clubs or vituperative match programme notes his weapons of choice. You might say that the late Doug Ellis of Aston Villa was a ‘football man’, yet Bates mocked the fact that a stand was named after him. When Villa built a new one for Euro ’96, he declared: ‘They're going to call it the Other Doug Ellis Stand.’

But there was a reason why the Chelsea Supporters' Trust issued a statement on Sunday declaring it was ‘deeply saddened’ by the death of Bates at his long-time home in Monaco. When he bought the club for £1 in 1982, they were on their knees -in deep financial trouble, struggling before crowds of 13,000 in the Second Division, to which they’d had been relegated three years earlier. Only the bank overdraft was keeping them in business.

The spending Bates sanctioned on Kerry Dixon, David Speedie, Pat Nevin and Mickey Thomas, bringing a joyous return to the First Division in 1984, formed the backdrop to an existential battle against a bigger enemy: the property company who owned the Stamford Bridge freehold and gave the club notice to quit in 1989.

Former Chelsea chairman and owner Ken Bates has died at the age of 94

Bates famously bought Chelsea for just £1, and sold the club to Roman Abramovich in 2003

Bates took over at Leeds United in 2005 after their relegation to the Championship

The ensuing legal struggle, which turned out to be Bates’ finest hour in football, was one that he, with his cussed, confrontational, litigious and sometimes deeply unpleasant style, was made for. It was when he’d won it that he had the vision to establish the Chelsea Pitch Owners, the supporter-led entity which preserved the stadium in perpetuity and remains one of the strongest protections of any fanbase in English football.

That combative style still made Bates a loathed figure among some at Chelsea, just like everywhere else. This was a time when hooliganism had the British game in its grip. Chelsea fans were involved in violent scenes at Derby County during the first year back in the First Division and their away fixtures were declared all-ticket for the remainder of the season. Bates’ solution was a 12 foot-high 12-volt electric perimeter fence at Stamford Bridge to deal with pitch invaders. It took Greater London council’s intervention to prevent this on safety grounds.

But his reinvention of Stamford Bridge as the Chelsea Village plc leisure complex was ahead of its time in broadening income streams, even though it is now viewed as an anchor on expanding the stadium at times. By the time he sold the club to Roman Abramovich for £140million in 2003, it had been reborn.

He used his ego and powers of persuasion to seek out those players he wanted for his club. This included asking Liverpool’s Graeme Souness for meeting at the Holiday Inn, on Liverpool’s Paradise Street in 1984, to see if he would sign for Chelsea. He offered Souness the use of a house he had on Guernsey and said he could just fly into London on a Thursday, to train and play. Souness turned him down, but the hiring of Ruud Gullit and Gianluca Vialli as managers, with Marcel Desailly, Gianfranco Zola, Roberto Di Matteo in their teams created a stardust without which Abramovich would not have arrived and turbocharged the ascent. Matthew Harding provided much of the money. Bates fell out with him too.

The £80m debt Bates racked up spoke of what was to follow in football for him, because parsimony and thrift were not in his lexicon and it would be a fight against the losses forever after.

His ambition at Leeds, relegated to the second tier and sinking under the debts accumulated in the Peter Ridsdale era when he arrived in 2005, was to replicate what he had achieved at Chelsea. But there was nothing more than turmoil, ceaseless litigation and open warfare with a fanbase whose reasonable demands for transparency led him to describe them as ‘morons.’

He cleared the debts by declaring the club insolvent, wiping away unsecured creditors. Players like Danny Mills, who had not played a competitive match for Leeds for four years, had to be paid the £216,667 owing to him in full, while the West Yorkshire ambulance service, owed £8,997, and St John Ambulance, £165, had to settle for a fraction. The ensuing 10-point deduction took Leeds down into League One, where a further 15-point penalty followed.

Bates, by then a tax-exile resident in Monaco, who owned Leeds via a company registered in the tax haven of Nevis, West Indies, unleashed on pretty much everyone in a bizarre series of programme notes after fans demanded an explanation for the running of their club and an understanding of who, other than Bates, actually owned it.

Bates, pictured with wife Suzannah, is remembered as one of English football's most controversial characters

Bates and former Chelsea manager Claudio Ranieri on pre-season tour in Malaysia in 2003

Bates helped bring glamour to Stamford Bridge in the 1990s with the arrival of Ruud Gullit

‘Educational standards have been destroyed by left-wingers and trendy liberals,’ he wrote in one programme. ‘Corporal and capital punishment should be brought back. Single mothers should be put into hostels and benefits slashed. This is a rather long way of saying that I am unimpressed by the demonstrations of a few morons last Saturday, and I ain't going anywhere soon.’

The qualities that made him admired by some at Chelsea - confrontation, financial pragmatism and a refusal to be intimidated - rendered him toxic at Leeds. As of last night, there had been no response from Leeds United or its fans to news of Bates’ death. None is expected.

His departure from that club in 2014 was followed by the widespread condemnation of his deeply unfortunate comments about a number of Chelsea youth-team footballers who had claimed they were racially abused by their own coaches during his 22-year tenure there. Bates claimed the ‘sniff of money is in the air.’

He will be remembered for controversies more than for the contribution he made to British football, though the clashes belie his long journey through the game. He had owned Oldham Athletic and Wigan Athletic before Chelsea and the myriad businesses he’d built his personal fortune from - haulage, quarrying, ready-mix concrete and dairy farming - also speak to a monumental energy.

Not bad, he would have said, for a boy raised by his grandparents in a council flat on a sink estate in Ealing, west London, whose hopes of playing football had been confounded by the club foot he was born with.

The conversations he and I had were of ‘journalistic interest’ in the perspective they provided from an individual who had lived in the white heat of the sport and was at the bridge to a new era of the unimaginable wealth he’d never known. ‘You’re only a custodian,’ he once said. ‘You’re there for a period of time and then someone else takes over.’

Sports.title: Bournemouth's Alex Jimenez joins Fiorentina on loan amid investigation into alleged messages with 15-year-old girl
Sports.content:
Bournemouth defender Alex Jimenez has joined Serie A club Fiorentina on a season-long loan amid an investigation into allegations he sent inappropriate messages to a 15-year-old schoolgirl.

The deal includes a €20million (£17m) option for Fiorentina to make the move permanent and allows the Spaniard to continue playing while suspended by Bournemouth pending the outcome of the investigation.

The 21-year-old has not played for the Cherries since the club launched an investigation on May 8 into a series of 'posts circulating on social media' that purportedly showed him exchanging messages with an underage girl.

It is alleged the messages included discussions about meeting up, with the female stating during the exchange that she was 15. There is no suggestion Jimenez ever met the girl.

Bournemouth confirmed in May that it had launched a probe into Jimenez, who signed a five-and-a-half-year deal with the club in February, and subsequently omitted him from the squad for their Premier League match against Fulham.

Jimenez has not played for the Cherries since the club launched an investigation on May 8 into a series of 'posts circulating on social media'

A club statement at the time said: 'AFC Bournemouth are aware of posts circulating on social media involving right-back, Alex Jimenez.

'The club understands the seriousness of the matter and it is currently being investigated.

'As a result, Alex will not be included in the squad for tomorrow's Premier League game against Fulham and the club will be making no further comment at this time.'

Jimenez remained unavailable for Bournemouth's final two matches of the season - 1-1 draws against Manchester City and Nottingham Forest - having featured in all but one of the club's league games before the investigation began.

The Spain Under 21 international started his career with Real Madrid Castilla, the Spanish giants' reserve side, before joining AC Milan in the summer of 2023.

He arrived at Bournemouth on an initial season-long loan in September before completing a permanent move five months later.

During his breakthrough campaign under Andoni Iraola, Jimenez made 32 appearances and scored his first goal for the club in a 3-2 home victory over Liverpool.

Sports.title: England must beat the heat AND Erling Haaland with Thomas Tuchel's side hit by sweltering 44 DEGREE Miami conditions after fears World Cup quarter final with Norway would be delayed
Sports.content:
Fears that England's crucial World Cup quarter-final showdown against Norway in Miami will be hit by delays or even postponement due to soaring temperatures across South Florida have been allayed.

A major heat risk had been declared in South Florida with temperatures said to be rising to 29-32°C - with a realfeel of up to 44°C - by the time today's game is due to kick off at 5pm in Miami (10pm UK time).

The City of Miami's official X account warned people in the local area to 'stay hydrated, wear lightweight clothing and limit outdoor activity'.

Their post read: 'Major Heat Risk is in effect across much of South Florida today.

'High temperatures and humidity can increase the risk of heat-related illness. Stay hydrated, wear lightweight clothing, limit outdoor activities during the hottest part of the day, and spend time in air-conditioned spaces whenever possible. Stay informed.'

FIFPRO, the global representative of professional footballers across the world, advise games should be delayed or postponed until conditions are safe if the local temperature exceeds 28°C.

England's crucial World Cup quarter-final showdown against Norway in Miami was at risk of being delayed due to dangerously high temperatures

Temperatures are soaring across South Florida ahead of kick-off at 5pm local time

A major heat risk has been declared in South Florida with temperatures said to be rising to 29-32°C

Daily Mail Sport understands, however, that there are currently no plans to change the kick-off time for tonight's game.

Both teams will still have to contend with sweltering temperatures in a stadium that, unlike some of its competitors at this tournament, is not air-conditioned and will not provide the respite players had in Dallas or Atlanta.

It will be the latest challenge for England's players after they battled inclement weather and altitude sickness in Mexico City.

England's last-16 match against Mexico was delayed by an hour during the early hours of Monday morning with the game kicking off at 2am (UK time) rather than 1am due to severe thunderstorms.

Supporters already at the stadium sought shelter, while media members were told they must not leave the media centre amid the yellow severe weather warning.

England's players arrived on schedule, raising hope that it would go ahead as planned at its original time, but that was quickly shelved just under an hour before it was due to kick-off.

Thomas Tuchel's side managed to overcome the elements and humidity to defeat the tournament co-hosts 3-2 and set up an encounter with Norway.

England fans have been given some good news today at least as supporters won't be kicked out of the pub if today's game is delayed.

The Government has now confirmed pubs can stay open in England and Wales until 30 minutes after the final whistle is blown, even if the start of the game is delayed.

Pictures show England supporters revelling at pool parties - with police needed to escort some out

England fans partying ahead of today's crunch quarter-final with Norway were left dripping wet after a tropical storm swept in bringing an end to outdoor parties

Ministers had already pushed opening hours for the game until 2am, but have made the extra extension with flexible licensing laws.

Policing minister Sarah Jones said: 'England fans deserve the chance to watch every minute of the quarter-final together, and that is exactly what our extension guarantees.

'After the weather delay we saw before the Mexico game, we want to give fans and venues complete certainty that no-one will miss a moment of the action.

'I hope pubs and bars across England and Wales are packed on Saturday night, as we hopefully move one step closer to bringing football home.'

The change has been made through new legislation temporarily extending licensing hours for eligible venues.

The same flexibility will apply to England's remaining matches, including the final, ensuring venues can stay open until 30 minutes after the final whistle if delays occur.

Sports.title: Revealed: The four England stars at risk of suspension for World Cup semi-final ahead of Norway clash
Sports.content:
Revealed: The four England stars at risk of suspension for World Cup semi-final ahead of Norway clash

How much is David Beckham set to pocket from his World Cup brand deals? Take on our quiz in our newsletter HERE

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

A clutch of England stars will have to be on their best behaviour should the Three Lions defeat Norway to book their spot in a World Cup semi-final.

Thomas Tuchel's side are preparing for a meeting with Erling Haaland & Co in Miami on Saturday night, and should the team gain a substantial lead, a place in the final four to play either Argentina or Switzerland could yet beckon.

But due to a change in FIFA's rules on player suspensions, some stars might be wary of their future involvement should England progress.

At this year's tournament, players will see the yellow cards they receive wiped at two points: after the group stage, and after the quarter-finals.

Previously, there was only one card amnesty ahead of the semi-finals, which might have meant that Declan Rice - who picked up a yellow during England's goalless draw with Ghana, and a second in their clash with Mexico - would not be available to face Norway.

Instead, Rice will be as wary as fellow team-mate Jude Bellingham, whose yellow card during England's round-of-32 tie versus DR Congo means that, should England progress, his participation could be under threat if he picks up another booking.

Jude Bellingham, Declan Rice, and Nico O'Reilly are among those on thin ice should England beat Norway

Nico O'Reilly is another star in a similar situation, as is his Manchester City team-mate Marc Guehi.

The former Crystal Palace defender was the recipient of a yellow card in the 68th minute against Mexico - which fans had erroneously thought was aimed in the direction of Harry Kane.

Rounding out the pack of players with one yellow card to their name is Jordan Henderson - although the Brentford midfielder is unlikely to constitute major suspension risk after sustaining a serious injury to his forearm in Mexico City.

The 36-year-old was caught up in England's raucous celebrations, vaulting over an advertising hoarding before landing awkwardly.

All four of those who have already picked up a yellow card between the round-of-32 and the quarter-final are expected to start in Miami.

Sports.title: Legendary BBC commentator announces shock retirement on air - following BBC's decision to axe Andrew Castle after 23 years
Sports.content:
Legendary BBC commentator announces shock retirement on air - following BBC's decision to axe Andrew Castle after 23 years

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Beloved BBC commentator John Lloyd confirmed live on air that he will head off into retirement after covering this summer's Wimbledon championships.

Lloyd, the BBC's famed tennis commentator, was calling the men's doubles final on Centre Court on Saturday as Henry Patten and Harri Heliovaara defeated Marcelo Arevalo and Mate Pavic.

The 71-year-old, who was a player himself in his heyday, has been with the BBC as a commentator since the 1990s.

While Lloyd wanted a low-key send off, his colleagues ensured that wasn't going to happen.

'Before we get to the presentation, worth just saying something about you, Lloyd-y,' his co-commentator Todd Woodbridge said.

To which the ever humble Lloyd replied: 'Wow, don't need to…'

Woodbridge had none of it, adding: 'It might be the last chance that I get to sit in the comms' box with you, it's been an absolute pleasure.'

'Thank you,' a touched Lloyd said. 'Yeah, it's very nice of you guys to say that.'

John Lloyd (centre, pictured in 2008) has called his last match as BBC's lead tennis commentator at Wimbledon having announced his shock retirement on Saturday afternoon

Woodbridge added: 'I look forward to meeting you up in the members' [area] later in the day each time when we come back, because you're not leaving.'

Lloyd said: 'That's for sure.'

It continues the dramatic evolution of the BBC's coverage for what is one of its most important events of the sporting calendar.

Sue Barker has long departed as lead presenter, while Andrew Castle was also cut prior to this latest championships as a lead commentator.

Now Lloyd, who famously married tennis legend Chris Evert in 1977 when both were players, will join them on the sidelines.

But while Lloyd has bowed out on his terms, the same could not be said for an 'upset' Castle.

Castle, a former top-100 player who had been the voice of the tournament for nearly 25 years, was dropped from the top job as the BBC looked to overhaul its coverage.

Head of BBC Sport, Alex Kay-Jelski, decided to take the corporation's coverage in a new direction, attempting to bring in new and younger audiences while cutting costs.

The corporation confirmed it wanted Castle to continue working for them in a different role, but he turned the offer down meaning this year will be his last.

Castle said prior to the championships that he would be upset during this year's tournament knowing it is his last but 'all good things must come to an end.'

Lloyd was a player in his heyday and also coached top British stars such as Sir Andy Murray

Andrew Castle, who has long commentated alongside Lloyd, will also be missing next year

The 62-year-old veteran broadcaster, who revealed he was leaving on June 16, said he wished he could have remained in the role until next year for the championship's 150th anniversary.

And to make the mood more dour, if Castle had made it one more year in the role, it would have been a special anniversary for him as well.

'It would have been my 25th year. But who's bleating?', he told the Daily Telegraph.

'I was told in person [about getting dropped], in a very respectful way, and I was very grateful for that – because knowing what I know about TV, you can be walking down the street one moment and the next you've been nobbled.'

Conor McGregor insists he can roll back the years tonight and rediscover his form, but the Irishman will have to overcome Max Holloway in order to do so

View Image Conor McGregor takes on Max Holloway tonight

Conor McGregor returns to the UFC tonight for his first fight in five years.

Sports.title: Noskova outlasts Muchova in Wimbledon final
Sports.content:
Open Extended Reactions

WIMBLEDON, England -- Linda Noskova is the latest in a long line of Czech women to win Wimbledon.

The 21-year-old Noskova recovered from a second-set meltdown in which she wasted five match points to overcome Karolina Muchova 6-2, 5-7, 6-3 in an all-Czech final on Saturday for her first Grand Slam trophy.

When Noskova finally won it with a service winner on her sixth match point, she covered her face and dropped down to the grass on her back.

"It's never easy to get the last point," Noskova said. "Karo, you really made me work for it."

Linda Noskova recovered from a second-set meltdown to overcome Karolina Muchova 6-2, 5-7, 6-3 in an all-Czech Wimbledon final for her first Grand Slam. Photo by Cameron Spencer/Getty Images

Noskova became the third Czech woman in four years to win the grass-court major, after Marketa Vondrousova in 2023 and Barbora Krejcikova in 2024.

Muchova and Noskova played doubles together at the 2024 Paris Olympics and finished fourth.

"I am so glad that I could play my first Grand Slam final with you," Noskova told Muchova during her victory speech. "We made history today. I believe that all our Czech fans at home are proud of us, so no matter the result today I think it was a good day for both of us."

Petra Kvitova, who won Wimbledon in 2011 and 2014, was in attendance, as was the greatest Czech-born player of them all, Martina Navratilova -- who won a record nine singles titles at the All England Club.

Navratilova looked on from the Royal Box, where she was seated next to Kate, the Princess of Wales, who presented the Venus Rosewater Dish trophy to Noskova.

Noskova grew emotional during her victory speech when she mentioned her mother, who died two years ago.

"I definitely would not be standing here without her, so thank you," said Noskova, who then looked up and blew a kiss to the sky.

Navratilova wiped away tears listening to Noskova's tribute to her mother.

Moments earlier, Muchova began her runner-up speech by calling Noskova "my ex-friend.

"I'm kidding, obviously," Muchova quickly added. "You're so young and this was your first final of a Grand Slam and the way you handled it ... was really unbelievable. ... You deserve it."

It was the 29-year-old Muchova's second Grand Slam final after getting beat by Iga Swiatek at the French Open in 2023.

In the men's final on Sunday, top-ranked Jannik Sinner will attempt to defend his title against French Open champion Alexander Zverev.

Wasted chances

Noskova led 5-2 in the second set before she lost five straight games to send it to a third.

When Noskova wasted a chance to serve it out at 5-3 in the second, she placed fingers in both ears to drown out the crowd noise on the changeover. Then she draped one of Wimbledon's strawberry-red towels over her head after she dropped her serve again to give Muchova a 6-5 lead and a chance for her opponent to serve it out -- which Muchova did.

It's Noskova's second grass title of the season after beating Jessica Pegula in the Berlin Open final three weeks ago.

But as this match displayed, it hasn't been all straightforward. Noskova saved a match point in the third set of her third-round match against Sorana Cirstea.

The 12th-ranked Noskova will climb to No. 7 -- a new career-high -- when the next rankings are released on Monday.

Jana Novotna, one of Noskova's first coaches, also won Wimbledon (in 1998).

Now Noskova is the youngest woman to win Wimbledon since Kvitova was also 21 in 2011.

And it marks the second consecutive Grand Slam won by a player 21 or younger after Mirra Andreeva claimed the French Open at 19 last month. It's the first time that's happened for Roland Garros and Wimbledon in the same year since Justine Henin and Serena Williams, respectively, claimed those titles in 2003.

Sports.title: Morant ready to 'start fresh' with Trail Blazers
Sports.content:
Open Extended Reactions

LAS VEGAS -- Ja Morant said Saturday that his offseason trade from the Memphis Grizzlies to the Portland Trail Blazers will give him the chance to "start fresh" and prove that his "bad guy" image is a misconception.

The two-time All-Star guard made four trips to the playoffs during his seven-year run with the Grizzlies, but his time in Memphis was complicated by a pair of gun-related suspensions in 2023.

"What would I like cleared up? I think you know the answer to that. My image. [That] I'm a bad guy," Morant said in his first public comments since the June trade. "I'm Ja. I've done what I've done in the past, but it's been addressed and handled already. I don't see why, years later, that's still the topic when nothing's happened since. If I was that guy, y'all wouldn't be talking to me now. I wouldn't be here."

Morant served an eight-game ban in March 2023 for conduct detrimental to the league and a 25-game suspension to open the 2023-24 season, both of which stemmed from incidents of him displaying a firearm on an Instagram livestream. The Grizzlies suspended him for one game in November because of a heated confrontation with coach Tuomas Iisalo after a loss to the Los Angeles Lakers.

The Blazers traded forwards Jerami Grant and Kris Murray for the 26-year-old Morant, who was the second pick in the 2019 NBA draft. Morant joins a talented and guard-heavy roster that includes Damian Lillard, Deni Avdija, Jrue Holiday, Scoot Henderson and Shaedon Sharpe.

"New home. New team. New organization," Morant said, wearing a black polo shirt with the team's logo as he addressed a handful of reporters at Las Vegas summer league. "I get to show the fans in Portland a different Ja. It's like starting all over again. ... Over the years, I've grown a lot and learned a lot. My mindset changed. I go into things differently now. I feel more mature, and I'm ready to work."

Morant, a South Carolina native who attended college in Kentucky, has some familiarity with his new home across the country: The Nike-sponsored athlete has made regular summer trips to the Portland area to visit the sneaker company's headquarters, and he said he once braved the Pacific Northwest rain to go fishing.

"[Portland] is a very quiet spot, it's nice," he said. "I don't know if you all have been paying attention to me lately, but I've been kind of into nature. I feel like that's a bonus. I'm not hiking, but I go walking, ride a bike, I've been kayaking. Just being grateful for being alive and the things I do have and my family. And to now have a fresh start. It's just mind clearing."

Morant averaged 19.5 points and 8.1 assists per game last season but was limited to just 20 games because of injuries. He said that his "body feels great," adding that he spent the last four months "making sure I was in shape and working" as trade rumors swirled.

Though Portland appears to have a backcourt logjam, Morant said he was willing to start or come off the bench, and he expressed excitement about playing with the likes of Lillard, Holiday and Avdija. Morant has spent time with several of his new teammates this week in Las Vegas.

"All those guys will most likely unlock new parts of my game, and I'll do the same for them," Morant said. "I don't think it will be a problem having us on the floor or making sure minutes match or anything. We're all very unselfish."

Morant expressed no ill will toward the Grizzlies, saying that Memphis will "always be home for me" and noting he is "still connected" with many of his former teammates.

Since the Grizzlies emerged as one of the league's most promising young cores during the 2022 playoffs, they have traded Morant, Jaren Jackson Jr. and Desmond Bane, and watched Dillon Brooks depart via free agency.

"[The reaction from Memphis] was all love," Morant said. "It's some [fans] that might say bad things about me. I don't look at it like it's hate or anything. I just look at it as tough love from a family member. I have family members that do the same thing. I love Memphis, I love the fans, I love my teammates. ... It definitely was some good years."

Sports.title: Day after cycle, White Sox OF Peters an All-Star
Sports.content:
Open Extended Reactions

CHICAGO -- Left-hander Justin Wrobleski became the sixth member of the World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers on the National League All-Star roster and Chicago outfielder Tristan Peters was added to the American League squad Saturday, a day after becoming the seventh White Sox player to hit for the cycle.

Wrobleski replaced Cincinnati right-hander Chase Burns, who won't be active for Tuesday night's game at Philadelphia's Citizens Bank Park.

Peters took the roster spot of Athletics first baseman Nick Kurtz, who was put on the injured list because of a sprained right thumb.

White Sox outfielder Tristan Peters, still a rookie at 26, is batting .303 with six homers and 35 RBIs, and on Friday became the seventh player in team history to hit for the cycle. Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images

Wrobleski, 26, is 10-2 with a 2.69 ERA and 73 strikeouts in 100⅓ innings. He joins two-way star Shohei Ohtani, right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto, first baseman Freddie Freeman, third baseman Max Muncy and outfielder Andy Pages as Dodgers All-Stars.

Ohtani will have his left knee drained Sunday to relieve continued irritation and will not go to Philadelphia.

Peters joins White Sox teammates Miguel Vargas and Munetaka Murakami on the All-Star roster. Murakami, a rookie slugger from Japan, was added Friday just hours before he returned to action against the Athletics after missing six weeks with a right hamstring strain.

Still a rookie at 26, speedy, slick-fielding Peters is batting .303 with six homers and 35 RBIs in his first full major league season. He has 20 doubles and three triples; the most recent came in the seventh inning of Chicago's rout of the Athletics on Friday that made Peters the first White Sox player to hit for the cycle since Jose Abreu in September 2017.

Chicago obtained Peters' rights last December from Tampa Bay. He appeared in only four games with the Rays last season without a hit in 12 plate appearances, but the one-time Savannah Banana has taken off in Chicago.

"The White Sox gave me this opportunity and I went into it just trying to make the most out of it and just be who I am as a player, too," Peters said. "I know there was a lot of bunting in the beginning and just trying to figure out who I am at the big league level and you know they give space for that, too. Just an incredibly supportive group and that's helped me thrive."

A native of Winkler, Manitoba, Peters became the second Canadian to record a cycle, joining George Kottaras. He also joins Cleveland right-hander Cade Smith and Miami infielder Otto Lopez, who holds dual Canadian and Dominican citizenship, as Canadians on the 2026 All-Star roster.

Peters said becoming an All-Star was a pipe dream at the start of the season. But after several months, he thought it might become a possibility.

"I guess toward the end of this first half, I was like 'OK, maybe there's a chance,' but there's a lot of really, really talented players in this league," he said.

Kurtz is batting .266 with 20 home runs, 66 RBIs and a league-leading 76 walks. The 23-year-old was the AL Rookie of the Year last season, when he batted .290 with 36 homers and 86 RBIs.

He landed on the injured list for the second time in his career, having been sidelined with a strained left hip flexor in May 2025.

Sports.title: Saint-Supery exits Gonzaga, signs with Valencia
Sports.content:
Open Extended Reactions

In a stunning move, Gonzaga starting point guard Mario Saint-Supery is returning to Spain.

On Saturday, EuroLeague squad Valencia announced that it had signed Saint-Supery, a point guard who earned all-West Coast Conference freshman honors after averaging 8.6 points per game last season, to a long-term deal.

Before his lone season at Gonzaga, Saint-Supery had earned the nickname "El Principito ("The Little Prince") as a standout in Spain's Liga ACB professional league.

"The Little Prince will make the Roig Arena his new palace," Valencia said in a release that also stated Saint-Supery would "continue his development at a high competitive level."

Saint-Supery wrote "Zag nation, thanks for everything" in an Instagram post on Saturday,

It's a significant move this late in the offseason for coach Mark Few's squad, which will play in the new Pac-12 in 2026-27. The transfer portal is closed and there are limited options to replace a talented point guard in July.

Saint-Supery, a 6-foot-4 athlete, made 40% of his 3-point attempts for the Bulldogs last year. He also started the final eight games of the season, a stretch that included a 21-point effort against Santa Clara in the WCC tournament title game. He also recorded 13 assists and four turnovers in two NCAA tournament games.

Along with Braden Huff, Davis Fogle and Arizona State transfer Massamba Diop, Saint-Supery was expected to be a floor general for a Gonzaga squad that will play outside the WCC for the first time since joining the league in 1979.

Saint-Supery's decision is not only a major move for the Bulldogs and their national title aspirations, but it's also an interesting signing amid a shifting landscape for international prospects.

Although the NCAA's 5-for-5 rule has been challenged in state courts, it has changed the outlook for international basketball players who want to play Division I hoops. Before the rule change, an international player's academic clock would begin only after they enrolled, but now the clock will start once they enroll in school or the academic year after they turn 19, whichever comes first. That will limit the time young international prospects will have to play at this level and end the trend of college teams adding older international players to their rosters.

The European landscape has lost multiple young prospects to college basketball teams during the NIL era.

On Saturday, a European squad took one back.

Sports.title: Bichette out again, may sit through All-Star break...
Sports.content:
Open Extended Reactions

NEW YORK -- Bo Bichette was held out of the lineup by the New York Mets on Saturday for a second straight day because of soreness in his legs and right ankle, and the infielder may sit through the All-Star break.

"It's a day-to-day thing," manager Andy Green said before the Mets continued a three-game series with the Boston Red Sox. "If he's feeling great tomorrow we'll get him back out there. If not we'll likely use the All-Star break to kind of get him a full reset."

Green said Bichette felt pain during last weekend's series in Atlanta when he went 8-for-18 but also fouled balls off his legs.

"In Atlanta, he fouled some balls off of his legs, kind of beat his legs up a little bit, played through a lot; the guy's a warrior," Green said. "Legs are just overall sore, got some right ankle soreness, as well, coupled with that."

Bichette went 0-for-3 in Thursday's 7-3 win over the Kansas City Royals and is hitting .320 with two homers and 11 RBIs in his last 25 games.

Overall, Bichette is hitting .256 with 10 homers and 51 RBIs in his first season with the Mets after seven seasons with the Blue Jays. He started this season by going 2-for-22 and was hitting .219 through the first two months.

The Mets signed Bichette to a $126 million, three-year contract in mid-January to play third base and he made the majority of his 44 starts at shortstop while Francisco Lindor was recovering from a calf strain. Bichette can opt out of the deal after the first or second season to become a free agent.

Infielder Semien nearing rehab assignment

Marcus Semien did some running Saturday after facing Clay Holmes in live batting practice Friday and could start a rehab assignment soon as the second baseman recovers from a left hip flexor strain.

Semien's rehab assignment may not occur until the end of the next week because the Mets' Triple-A and Double-A teams are off during the All-Star break.

"Obviously, it's tough timing with the All-Star break," Green said. "Only games going on are in the FCL through the All-Star break and I've seen too many of those games in the last few years to feel great about putting our hitters in the batter's box."

Semien was placed on the 10-day injured list June 25 and has missed 16 games. Acquired from Texas for Brandon Nimmo in November, Semien is batting .214 with nine homers and 29 RBIs in 80 games.

Sports.title: ✍️ Grading the Spurs' max deal for Wemby, more
Sports.content:
Open Extended Reactions

The NBA offseason is here, and teams across the league have been busy making moves. Free agency officially began Tuesday night.

I'm grading every free agent signing and the most impactful extensions this offseason, breaking down the ramifications for all teams and players involved.

To determine each grade, I'm looking at multiple factors, including the player's on-court impact and age, the contract's financial implications and the context of the team's short- and long-term outlooks. How risky or certain is the move? And how much does it help or hurt the team's chance to win a championship, next season or beyond?

Let's get into the latest moves:

Quick links:

Trade grades | Latest buzz | Trade machine

Depth charts | Trade tracker | More coverage

Victor Wembanyama terms: Five years, $252 million

Grade: A+

This might be the easiest transaction I'll ever grade.

Before last season, 83% of the NBA's general managers chose Wembanyama as the player they'd most like to build a franchise around. And that number has probably risen since, as Wembanyama was the unanimous Defensive Player of the Year, finished third in MVP voting and was the best player on a Finals team in 2025-26.

The Spurs would have received an "A" grade for extending Wembanyama no matter the contract details. He could have received the max, a player option and "Rose rule" salary escalator language, and Spurs brass would have been thrilled.

But in the end, he did not take every possible bell and whistle allowed for a player of his experience level, which boosts this grade to an "A+" for the Spurs.

According to ESPN's Shams Charania, Wembanyama is locking himself into a 25% maximum contract. He could have chosen an extension that would rise to 30% of the cap if he received postseason honors next year -- which seems like a virtual lock if Wembanyama reaches the 65-game minimum for awards consideration again.

Many other young stars have opted for that latter route in recent years, and they deserve no blame for maximizing their earnings. Evan Mobley, for instance, landed a 30% supermax before winning Defensive Player of the Year in 2025.

But Wembanyama has evidently taken a lesson from the star guard who beat the Spurs in the Finals last month, after the Knicks' title run was aided in part by Jalen Brunson's decision to sacrifice some of his own potential earnings to help New York build a championship roster.

The difference between 25% and 30% of the cap projects as $8.7 million next season, per ESPN's Bobby Marks, and that gap would grow over the course of Wembanyama's extension to a total of $50 million over five years. Now, the Spurs can use those savings to extend Stephon Castle and Dylan Harper, and still bolster the rotation around those young stars.

July 8: Post to join Grizzlies on offer sheet

Quinten Post terms: Three years, $30 million

Grade: B-

Post made a little bit of history with this contract, as the Warriors chose not to match Memphis's offer sheet to retain their 7-footer. It represents the first time a restricted free agent's original team didn't match an offer sheet since 2020, when Bogdan Bogdanovic left the Kings for the Hawks, according to ESPN's Bobby Marks.

That decision made sense for Golden State. Post is far younger than Al Horford and Kristaps Porzingis, but his stretch big skill set is duplicative next to those veteran spacers. And more importantly, this level of financial commitment would have been punishing for the Warriors, who are hard-capped at the first apron and still have a fair bit of summer business -- re-signing Draymond Green and potentially adding LeBron James -- to accomplish before reaching that barrier.

For the Grizzlies, however, fitting Post into their cap sheet is a relatively easy feat after they traded the more expensive Santi Aldama. Post, 26, is a lesser version of Aldama on offense but a superior defender; opponents have made 58% of their shots at the rim against Post in his career, per NBA Advanced Stats, which is a solid number for a reserve big.

Whether Post is actually a formidable stretch big is a more worrying question for Memphis, as his 3-point accuracy fell from 41% in his rookie season to just 34% last year. And with Zach Edey and the recently acquired Isaiah Stewart also on the roster, to say nothing of No. 3 pick Cameron Boozer and the recently acquired Jerami Grant and Taylor Hendricks, Memphis is chock-full of players who are best suited to play the 4 and 5.

Post brings a unique element in that group because of his combination of size and shooting. But if Edey can stay on the court next season, it's unclear how much Post will actually play.

Donovan Mitchell terms: Four years, $273 million

Grade: B-

Mitchell is a consistently excellent NBA superstar. He has been an All-Star in each of the past seven seasons and a first- or second-team All-NBA honoree in three of his four years in Cleveland.

The Cavaliers gave up a haul in their blockbuster trade for Mitchell in 2022, and they have to be mostly pleased with the results. Even if they haven't reached the Finals with Mitchell, they've been a consistent contender with him aboard.

And with Darius Garland now traded, James Harden well past his prime and Evan Mobley stuck on a developmental plateau, Mitchell remains the team's clear No. 1 option even as he approaches his 30th birthday. With two seasons left on his current contract, including a player option in 2027-28, there was an imperative for Cleveland to extend Mitchell now, lest he decline his option and leave in free agency next summer.

But that logistical reality doesn't make this new contract any more comfortable for Cleveland. Mitchell's maximum extension will start at $60.9 million in 2027-28, per ESPN's Bobby Marks, and will run through his age-34 season in 2030-31, when he'd be projected to hold a player option for $75.5 million.

This extension is a gamble that Mitchell will enjoy an elongated prime, but that's a risky proposition. He's a relatively small guard who regularly misses time each season, though he admittedly hasn't suffered any severe injuries; he's played between 53 and 71 games every year since 2018-19.

He also seems to wear down by the postseason and struggles to maintain his form when the games matter most. Mitchell famously reached the conference finals for the first time this spring, but he was far from his best self -- his true shooting fell from 61% in the regular season to 56% in the playoffs -- along the way.

Devoting such a high percentage of the salary cap to a second-tier star -- someone who makes All-NBA teams but never seriously contends for MVP -- complicates a team's roster-building options in the NBA's current financial environment. In a world in which the Celtics struggled to find any trade partners for Jaylen Brown, who's owed an average of $61.7 million over the next three seasons, a new contract for Mitchell at an average of $68.2 million per season is similarly daunting.

Cleveland's new pact with Mitchell is similar to the Suns' deal with Devin Booker, who signed an extension last summer that will pay him an estimated $68.8 million in his age-33 season in 2029-30. Mitchell has experienced higher highs than Booker, who has been a top-10 player (in All-NBA terms) only once. But they're in the same broad category of star guards who probably can't be the best player on a championship team.

That probably qualifier is important, because Jalen Brunson just provided proof of concept for a small scoring guard to win Finals MVP. The Cavaliers hope Mitchell can pull off the same feat at some point during the span of his new contract -- preferably on the earlier side, before he reaches his mid-30s with an escalating salary.

But Mitchell is a rung below Brunson in terms of postseason pedigree, and, crucially, Brunson signed a below-market extension to help New York construct a robust roster around him.

Mitchell doesn't deserve any blame for not taking as much money as he could -- but the fact of the matter is that his new extension, combined with Cleveland's already-limited resources, won't make it any easier for the Cavaliers to improve in the near future, when they most need that improvement to take advantage of Mitchell's remaining prime.

Rui Hachimura terms: Two years, $28 million

Grade: B+

Hachimura's $14 million per year places him in the middle of several other power forward types who have signed in free agency this summer: John Collins at $17 million annually, Tobias Harris at $15.5 million and Sandro Mamukelashvili at $13 million.

Compared with that group, Hachimura has the best singular standout skill. After a poor start to his career from long range, Hachimura has developed into an excellent shooter. Over his three full seasons with the Lakers, he made 42.6% of his 3-pointers, which ranked second (behind Luke Kennard) out of 216 players with at least 500 attempts in that span.

The rest of Hachimura's game isn't so special, which is why he's not at the top end of the power forward market. He's a sturdy defender because of his size (6-foot-8, 230 pounds), but not a game changer on that end of the floor, and he has never created many shots for others (0.8 assists per game last season, 1.2 per game in his career).

For the Clippers, Hachimura represents a low-risk floor-raiser after the team turned over its entire roster over the past few years. And while Hachimura might have made more sense for a contender, where his shooting could have made a real difference as a supplement to stars -- as it did with the Lakers during their conference finals run in 2023 -- he preferred to stay in Los Angeles, per ESPN's Shams Charania. That sounds like a win-win deal.

July 3: Drummond to Knicks as champs find a center

Andre Drummond terms: One year, $3.9 million

Grade: B-

Stylistically, the Knicks couldn't have found a better replacement for Mitchell Robinson. He and Drummond are massive centers, indefatigable rebounders and poor free throw shooters.

Robinson is the best offensive rebounder in the NBA, but so too was Drummond, once upon a time. He led the league in offensive boards per game from 2013-14 through 2019-20, and his per-36 numbers remain similar to this day. When Drummond enters games, he'll give the Knicks this same offensive advantage that Robinson did.

But this is a qualitative downgrade for the Knicks. There's a reason that Robinson commanded a $47.4 million contract over three years, while Drummond signed for the veteran minimum.

Notably, Drummond is a worse defender. He allowed opponents to shoot 68% at the rim last season, one of the worst marks for a center, while Robinson was at 58%. That difference could be an issue in the playoffs, where such weaknesses are magnified and Drummond hasn't had much success; he won the first series of his career this spring, when the Philadelphia 76ers upset the Boston Celtics.

If the Knicks were never going to go into the second apron for any reason, as owner James Dolan suggested, then they couldn't have afforded to retain Robinson. Drummond is a worthy replacement in that context. But if Karl-Anthony Towns is in foul trouble in a crucial moment next postseason and the Knicks have Drummond playing big minutes, New York might regret this financially motivated roster change.

Neemias Queta terms: Four years, $56 million

Grade: A-

The same advanced stats that have so riled up Celtics fans in recent weeks due to their mild skepticism of Jaylen Brown positively adore Queta. xRAPM ranks Queta in the 96th percentile of players in per-possession impact, and estimated plus-minus ranks him in the 95th percentile.

That's pretty good for a former two-way player who had never reached 1,000 minutes in a season before 2025-26. But Queta was extraordinary stepping into Boston's vacated starting center role, averaging 10.2 points, 8.4 rebounds and 2.1 stocks (steals plus blocks) per game. Most importantly, the Celtics had a plus-13.2 net rating with him on the floor, the highest mark on the team.

The Celtics extended Queta for the long term with a two-step maneuver. First, they exercised his $2.7 million team option for 2026-27, giving the team extra financial flexibility for next season -- which they used to sign Mitchell Robinson, another center with excellent advanced stats. And second, they inked Queta to a four-year extension that will start in 2027-28, keeping him in Boston through his prime.

Especially given other, more expensive contracts handed out to centers this offseason, Queta's new deal looks like a bargain for Boston, if his performance last season is any indication of the half-decade to come. Only two small nuggets of concern drop this grade from an A to an A-minus.

First, Queta has a relatively short track record of that level of play. And second, he struggled in the postseason as Boston lost in seven games against Philadelphia. It remains to be seen whether Queta functions better as a regular-season innings-eater or a championship-level contributor.

Tari Eason terms: Five years, $81.5 million

Grade: A

The NBA's current cap environment is designed to punish complacency. In previous eras, teams could prioritize good feelings and round up on their contract offers -- giving a slightly sub-max player the max, proposing an extra year or a player option, and so on.

But not anymore. Now, every dollar beneath the apron counts, and flexibility is the new guiding light. Front offices must be cutthroat rather than complacent if they want to build a sustainable winning roster over the long term.

It has taken some time to adapt to that new state of affairs, and even now, not every team has made the adjustment. But the Rockets have been one of the new model teams in how to negotiate with their own players: Kevin Durant, Alperen Sengun, Jalen Green and Fred VanVleet all signed deals with some team-friendly elements, rather than their individual maximums.

They did it again with Eason, one of the best 3-and-D prospects in the league. The 6-foot-8 Eason is a phenomenal defender with positional versatility, and he and Amen Thompson -- who's eligible for a rookie contract extension of his own this summer -- could continue harassing opposing guards and wings for years to come.

He has also improved on the offensive end, even if that will never be his greatest strength. Last season, Eason made a career-best 36% of his 3-pointers on a career-high number of attempts (though his 2-point percentage plummeted at the same time).

Perhaps most importantly, Eason has been mostly healthy for two seasons in a row, which assuages the greatest concern about his profile: He played just 22 games in 2023-24, but he has increased his availability to 57 and 60 games over the last two seasons.

At just over $16 million per year for a player with his skill set and potential, this could end up as one of the best value contracts signed by any player this summer. At the very least, a version of Eason who's locked in for half a decade at this price should be very attractive in a trade, if the Rockets ever decide to make him available in a deal for another star.

And at the most, he'll deliver tremendous value to Houston over the course of this deal, as the Rockets use the added flexibility from their hard bargains to continue upgrading their roster and constructing a contender.

Anfernee Simons terms: Two years, $12.3 million (player option in second year)

Grade: C+

Simons is one of the NBA's premier microwave scorers, the spiritual heir to the likes of Lou Williams and Jamal Crawford. With the Celtics last season, he averaged 14.2 points in 24.5 minutes per game while making 39.5% of his 3-pointers, before a trade to Chicago and a wrist injury ended his season.

He'll now serve as the 76ers' third guard, replacing the departed Quentin Grimes, who signed a much larger deal (four years, $60 million) with the Lakers. Equally capable of spotting up on the perimeter or running a pick-and-roll on his own, Simons should give Philadelphia instant offense off the bench.

But this is a curious fit because of Simons' ineffectiveness on the other end. He's a small guard whom advanced stats rank as one of the NBA's worst defenders. So it's unclear whether he'll be able to play next to Tyrese Maxey without compromising Philadelphia's defense beyond repair.

It's also unclear what Simons' arrival means for No. 22 pick Labaron Philon Jr., another small guard with defensive question marks. Philon weighed 176 pounds at the NBA combine, which made him the lightest player taken in the first round. For that reason, it's difficult to imagine him and Simons playing together in bench units. Perhaps that doesn't matter much to the 76ers, who have more pressing win-now demands following the Jaylen Brown trade. It's unlikely that a rookie guard taken after the lottery will help a contender next year, anyway.

But with Brown and VJ Edgecombe able to soak up much of the playmaking duties when Maxey goes to the bench, if Philadelphia staggers its best perimeter players, Simons seems like more of an oddly fitting luxury than a player who fills a glaring need. His signing brings the 76ers within $4 million of the first apron hard cap, and one wonders whether they could have found a more compelling use of their remaining space.

Kelly Oubre Jr. terms: Two years, $17 million

Grade: B

No NBA team can have enough 3-and-D wings. That role is too valuable and too versatile. So, on the surface, adding Oubre to a group that already includes Aaron Nesmith, Andrew Nembhard and Ben Sheppard makes all the sense in the world.

It is worth asking how many members of that group are actually reliable shooters. Nesmith is a given, at 39.6% from distance over four seasons in Indiana. But there's a curious trend with the other three members of Indiana's wing rotation. Player Career before 2025-26 2025-26 Kelly Oubre Jr. 32.5% 36.0% Andrew Nembhard 33.5% 36.1% Ben Sheppard 33.0% 36.2%

Oubre, Nembhard and Sheppard were all around 33% in their careers before last season, which is quite poor. But then they all improved to reach league-average accuracy. Oubre's jump was particularly notable because he had the greatest subpar track record heading into 2025-26; he shot a career-high 36% just one year after shooting 29% from distance.

There's a potential downside here: If Oubre, Nembhard and Sheppard all regress to their career norms next season, Indiana's offense might not improve as much as expected with the return of Tyrese Haliburton because they'll miss a lot of 3s on kickout passes from their star point guard.

But if the trio's league-average performance from distance is more than a one-year fluke, then Indiana might just have enough for a Finals return.

July 1: Spurs sign wing Tobias Harris

Tobias Harris terms: Two years, $31 million

Grade: A-

The Spurs had a number of mid-30s veterans on their roster last season, but they contributed much more off the court than via their actual play on it. Harrison Barnes played only 17 minutes in the Finals, and Bismack Biyombo, Kelly Olynyk and Mason Plumlee didn't play at all.

So, San Antonio entered the offseason with two holes to fill: on-court veteran experience and a two-way power forward with more size than Julian Champagnie and more skill than Carter Bryant, after the likes of OG Anunoby and (briefly) Julius Randle presented problems in the postseason. Enter Tobias Harris.

Harris will turn 34 later this month, and he has never made an All-Star team or received end-of-season awards votes of any kind. But he remains a well-above-average contributor because of his consistency and all-around play.

Harris is almost always available, having appeared in at least 62 games in each of the past dozen seasons. He's a viable 3-point shooter (37% both in his career and last season) who can create his own shot in a pinch, and he's a solid rebounder and defender.

Above all, Harris' teams have been better with him on the court in six of the past seven seasons, per Cleaning the Glass -- never by a gigantic amount but consistently enough to form a recognizable trend.

Even at his age, that sort of production should be worth more than $15.5 million per season. It's possible that the Spurs could have found a superior free agent option for their midlevel exception; Rui Hachimura's shooting advantage over Harris could make him a better fit in San Antonio, for instance.

But because the Spurs' contracts will grow much more expensive in the next few years, as their top-five picks start receiving extensions, they had an incentive to limit the years on their contracts this summer. And Harris' age evidently made him amenable to signing for just two years, even as other players in this range sign for longer (see, for instance, Sandro Mamukelashvili's and Dean Wade's four-year pacts with the Lakers and 76ers, respectively).

By signing Harris at this price, the Spurs got better, and they got a bargain, simultaneously.

July 1: Celtics sign former Knicks big Mitchell Robinson

Mitchell Robinson terms: Three years, $47.4 million (player option in third year)

Grade: B+

Boston likes to shoot 3-pointers, and Robinson has never even attempted -- let alone made -- a 3. But this signing is an example of the Celtics doubling down on a strength, regardless.

With Neemias Queta replacing Al Horford and Kristaps Porzingis as the Celtics' primary center last season, they added a new wrinkle to their offense in an effort to win the possession battle. They ranked fifth in offensive rebounding rate, their first time in the top 10 under Joe Mazzulla.

And it just so happens that Robinson is one of the best offensive rebounders in NBA history. Among players with at least 5,000 career minutes, Robinson is tied for second (with Dennis Rodman) in career offensive rebounding rate.

That's just one of several fascinating elements to this signing, which sends a key player from the champs to one of their biggest rivals. This isn't a consideration notable enough to affect many free agent grades, but the fact that the Celtics not only added Robinson, but simultaneously took him away from the second-apron-averse New York Knicks adds to their score.

Robinson is a unique player with both obvious strengths and just as obvious weaknesses. He'll offer Boston unparalleled second-chance opportunities, rim protection and much-needed above-the-rim athleticism, and he'll also frustrate Celtics fans with his free throw struggles and inconsistent availability.

In games between the Celtics and Knicks, Mazzulla was one of the most frequent Hack-a-Mitch practitioners, as Robinson's woes at the charity stripe only grew more extreme. He made just 41% of his free throws in the 2025-26 regular season, and an even worse 29% in the playoffs.

The Knicks' fear of Robinson free throws often kept him off the floor. So did various injuries, as Robinson's 60 games last season were his most since 2021-22; in the two previous years, he played just 48 regular-season games combined.

But Boston has the depth to manage Robinson's minutes carefully throughout the regular season, and his new team is really hoping he raises its ceiling in the playoffs. Queta excelled in the starting lineup last season -- up until the playoffs, when he lost his way against Philadelphia. Robinson is an NBA champion who won't be cowed by the moment next spring.

De'Antony Melton terms: Two years, $11 million (player option in second year)

Grade: A

Last summer, Melton signed a two-year deal with the Warriors, with a player option in the second year. He opted out and is going the same route this summer, just with a slightly higher price tag following a strong comeback season from a torn ACL in November 2024.

Regardless of whether the Warriors' star ambitions pan out this summer, Melton will be an excellent fit on their roster as a do-it-all guard with a knack for forcing turnovers. He doesn't need the ball to contribute, and if his 3-point shot bounces back with more time removed from his injury -- he was at 29% last season, a big step down from his previous 37% career mark -- he'll thrive playing off Stephen Curry (and LeBron James?).

The Warriors had a plus-3.9 net rating with Melton on the court last season, which ranked second on the team behind Jimmy Butler III. Still only 28 years old, he's squarely in his prime.

Perhaps he'll turn in another solid season and do the "opt out and re-sign" dance with Golden State once again next summer.

Quentin Grimes terms: Four years, $60 million

Grade: B-

Sandro Mamukelashvili terms: Four years, $52 million

Grade: B

Collin Sexton terms: Two years, $19 million (player option in second year)

Grade: B-

The Lakers piled all of their offseason activity into one hectic hour. After coming to an agreement on a blockbuster trade for center Walker Kessler, they signed these three role players in quick succession, dramatically reconfiguring their roster around Luka Doncic and Austin Reaves.

LeBron James, Rui Hachimura, Marcus Smart and Luke Kennard were the top four Lakers in minutes played last postseason, but all four are now out, while Grimes, Mamukelashvili and Sexton are in. So what does that exchange mean for the Lakers' present and future?

Grimes is the cleanest fit of the bunch, so he naturally received the biggest payday. After uneven stints in New York, Detroit and Dallas -- where he was Doncic's teammate for half a season -- he broke out in Philadelphia, averaging 15.7 points in 30.6 minutes per game.

After playing behind Tyrese Maxey and VJ Edgecombe last season, and behind Doncic and Kyrie Irving before that, Grimes is intimately familiar with the role of a third guard, which he'll occupy behind Doncic and Reaves in Los Angeles. He might even start with the Lakers, because of their two stars' size.

Grimes doesn't fill the 3-and-D archetype, because he's both too small to guard top-tier wings and not an accurate enough shooter (33.4% on 3s last season, 36.6% in his career) to stretch opposing defenses. But because Doncic and Reaves aren't going to defend point guards, Grimes can capably take on that assignment every night, and he'll help with secondary creation when either of the stars rests.

When the Lakers execute the below transactions on July 6, they will need to renounce all their free agents (except of course Austin Reaves). https://t.co/Phr8Ft086G — Bobby Marks (@BobbyMarks42) July 1, 2026

Sexton, conversely, will stretch opposing defenses, as he has made between 39.3% and 40.6% of his 3-pointers in each of the past four seasons. That's not quite at Kennard's level, but on a Lakers roster that could be starved for shooting, he could play a major role in preventing opposing defenses from collapsing on Doncic-Kessler pick-and-rolls.

Sexton's $9.5 million per year is right in line with the going rate for shooters this offseason, and he offers more on-ball juice than so-called pure shooters with more singular skill sets.

Can the Lakers survive defensively if Sexton plays alongside Doncic and Reaves? That's a less promising prospect. But coach JJ Redick's scheme managed to protect a collection of subpar defenders last season -- the trio of Doncic, Reaves and Kennard posted a league-average defensive rating in 175 minutes together -- so it's at least feasible.

Finally, the Mamukelashvili signing might have the highest ceiling and lowest floor from this flurry of free agent deals. I'm a big believer in Mamukelashvili, who finally got a chance to play real minutes last season and broke out to the tune of 11.2 PPG and a 39% 3-point stroke for the Raptors. He rates well by advanced stats and still appears to have untapped potential.

Mamukelashvili did most of that work as a center, where he played 61% of his minutes, per Cleaning the Glass. Toronto had a plus-9.4 net rating with him at center, versus a minus-1.1 net rating with him at power forward. That might say more about the Raptors as a team than about Mamukelashvili as an individual, but his ability to space the floor is much less unique when he's playing power forward.

Yet it still seems as if the Lakers, with Kessler in the fold, plan to use Mamukelashvili more as a power forward. That's a better match for his defensive ability, but could sap some of what makes him special. And if Mamukelashvili is effectively replacing Hachimura in the rotation, even he can't measure up to Hachimura's elite shooting ability.

The end result from all of these moves is a roster with much more offensive ability next to Doncic and Reaves, but a paucity of defense around that already offensively inclined duo. Grimes is a strong defender, but small, and Sexton and Mamukelashvili are weak links on that end. Adding Kessler, one of the NBA's top rim protectors, will help, but he'll have to compensate for an extreme weakness on the perimeter.

Norman Powell terms: Two years, $45 million

Grade: B-

Zach Collins terms: Two years, $17 million

Grade: C-

The Bulls entered the offseason with more than $50 million in cap space, and they've essentially used it all. First, they traded for Nic Claxton, and then they signed Powell and re-signed Collins.

The Claxton trade received a B-minus grade. Find the full analysis at this link, but the crux of my assessment was: "Taking on his contract into their cap space means it's fair to treat the Bulls' end of this three-team deal as if they were signing Claxton to a two-year, $44 million contract. That would be decent but not overwhelming value, and their grade here reflects that tradeoff."

The same sentiment -- decent but not overwhelming value -- applies to Powell's new contract, which is strange insofar as it brings one of the only All-Star free agents to a rebuilding team, rather than a win-now contender.

Chicago is entering a new era, with a new general manager, a new coach and a roster built around 19-year-old Caleb Wilson and 21-year-old Matas Buzelis. Powell, conversely, is 33 years old, and even though he's peaking late -- the past two seasons are arguably the best of his career -- he's unlikely to be part of the next winning Bulls team.

To be fair, there is value in competence, especially in the new lottery era. With Powell on board, the Bulls seem destined to finish with between the fourth- and 10th-worst record in the league -- which would maximize their lottery odds -- rather than as one of the three worst teams. And Powell's shooting (40% on 3s in his career) and individual shot creation should create space for Wilson and Buzelis to operate and grow their games.
